label: John Milton, Paradise Lost (1667; 2nd ed. 1674)
text: The first of the three books the Creature finds. He later reads Adam's and Satan's stories against his own; the novel's epigraph comes from Book X.

label: Plutarch, Parallel Lives (c. 100 CE)
text: Paired biographies of Greek and Roman statesmen; for the Creature, a first lesson in public virtue.

label: Goethe, The Sorrows of Young Werther (1774)
text: Goethe's novel in letters. The spelling “Werter” is that of the early English versions; the first (1779) was translated from the French.

text: Crusoe's single footprint on the shore of his island, here the one bare print an invisible foot leaves on a London doorstep.

loc.exact: in a place that doctor Swift would have named

label: Jonathan Swift, Gulliver's Travels (1726)
text: Swift is named as the writer who would not have spared the ladies the word. In Gulliver's Travels the Lilliputian mathematicians take the giant's height “by the help of a quadrant”; here the mites take the Sirian's “with sight-vanes pointed at a quarter circle” as he lies flat. The Kehl editors, quoted in Beuchot's preface, call the tale “an imitation of Gulliver's Travels.”

label: Jonathan Swift, Gulliver's Travels (1726)
text: Lilliput is the country of tiny people in the first voyage of Gulliver's Travels, where Gulliver wakes bound by “a human creature not six inches high” and his fellows. Here the Square, a giant beside the Linelanders, hears their whole kingdom as the chirping of insects, as Gulliver hears the voices of Lilliput.

loc.exact: from the white whale, the terrible “Moby Dick” of hyperborean regions

label: Herman Melville, Moby-Dick (1851)
text: The white whale Ahab hunts, the one he describes to his crew as having “a wrinkled brow and a crooked jaw” and “three holes punctured in his starboard fluke.” Verne's papers set it beside the kraken among the monsters a sober public laughs at; a few pages later Ned Land is called “the prince of harpooners.”
